summary:
Angola's decriminalisation of same-sex conduct took effect on 11 February 2021. The statute adopted in 2019 overturned the colonial-era provision describing same-sex relationships as a 'vice against nature' and, in the same instrument, made discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation punishable by imprisonment. A continental survey published in October 2019 rated Angola as having gone furthest among African reforms of that period, both by removing the colonial offence and by attaching penalty to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services.

The constitutional layer is thinner than the statutory one. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre's chapter on transgender rights in Angola records that Article 23 of the Constitution does not list gender or sexual orientation among the prohibited grounds of discrimination, while the rights of identity, privacy, liberty, protection from torture and freedom of expression are located across Title II of the same document. A visitor therefore has statutory protection against orientation-based discrimination but no explicit constitutional guarantee on grounds of gender identity.

No specific law allows transgender people to change their gender marker on official documents and passports. Section 78 of the Código do Registo Civil 2015 states that, in general, there should be no alteration of details entered into registration records; section 87, however, gives the Civil Registrar general authority to make changes, including changes of name and where a change of facts alters a person's legal identity and status. The Southern Africa Litigation Centre reads this as a possible route for transgender people to change their legal gender, but it is a discretionary administrative power rather than a trans-specific procedure, and no case law or practice is recorded. A 2017 ILGA poll found that 49% of Angolans believed transgender people should be allowed to change their legal gender.

There is no legal recognition of same-sex couples in Angola. Social pressure to marry a partner of the opposite sex is significant: in 2005 an unofficial same-sex commitment ceremony was reported as 'shameless' and 'abominable' in national news magazines. Visitors in relationships should not expect any partner-based rights, next-of-kin standing or hospital access deriving from that relationship.

Documentation of abuse continues through regional and UN channels. A shadow report on Angola's compliance with the African Charter, submitted for the African Commission's 81st session in October and November 2024 in Banjul by Angolan organisations including Arquivo de Identidade Angolano, IRIS Angola, I am Trans Movement, ASTA and Diversidade Masculina with ILGA and Synergia support, documents human-rights violations against LGBTQI+ people. Separately, Angolan LGBTQI+ organisations made a submission to the UN Committee on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights ahead of the 74th session's review of Angola, raising discrimination and health-access issues affecting lesbian, bisexual, transgender, intersex and queer people.

Legal entitlements in health are stated clearly for people living with HIV/AIDS, who are entitled to health care services and to protection from employment discrimination. No shelters, safe houses, gender-neutral facilities or other dedicated facilities for LGBTQ people are recorded anywhere in the sources, so a visitor should not expect dedicated safe accommodation or identity-affirming facilities to be available.

No entry or visa provisions for Angola are recorded in these sources. The only entry-adjacent material consists of external reference links: an asylumlaw.org packet on sexual minorities and HIV status used for asylum purposes, and UK Foreign & Commonwealth Office travel advice on local laws and customs. Entry requirements are therefore not established by this inventory.

Visible trans presence has existed alongside formal criminalisation. In April 2012 the kuduro singer Titica, born male and presenting female, became a mainstream star at 25, in what the BBC described as a Catholic country where homosexuality was then illegal and punishable by hard labour. That account predates the 2021 decriminalisation and describes the earlier regime.

Civic space for LGBTQ organisations is present but narrow. Two LGBT groups operate in Angola and only one, the Iris Angola Association, has received official and legal recognition, granted by the Angolan Justice Ministry in June 2018; at that time it had about 200 members, based in Luanda with offices in Benguela and Lubango. The three major political parties have not formally addressed LGBT issues in their platforms. The government does allow non-governmental organisations to exist, and some charities have begun working with LGBT community members on HIV/AIDS education.
tangentialFactors:
Angola's 2019 statute is repeatedly cited as the leading African reform of its period, both for deleting the colonial offence and for attaching imprisonment to orientation-based discrimination in employment and services. Comparisons of legislative drafting strategies across the continent are drawn from that reform.

In 2010 the Angolan Government refused to receive openly gay Isi Yanouka as the new Israeli ambassador, allegedly because of his sexual orientation. This was a decision about who was invited to a diplomatic reception, not a visa or entry rule, and it should not be read as an entry restriction.

Education-focused work for LGBTQ Angolans is nascent and underfunded. The first association, Acção Humana (Human Action), launched in 2006 but has been unable to receive funding, and efforts to develop educational programmes specifically for LGBT people have struggled to attract NGO funding. An HIV/AIDS educational programme for LGBT people is only beginning to develop through NGOs such as Population Services International, and a 2007 study estimated roughly five percent of HIV infections were among men who have sex with men.
